newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu vows to defend settlements on U.S. trip.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu vows to defend settlements on U.S. trip.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu will insist during a U.S. visit next week on Israel's "right" to settle Jews in Jerusalem and the West Bank despite violent Arab protests, his spokesman said on Thursday.

"The prime minister will make clear in Washington that Israel stands by its right to build in Jerusalem and in settlements, and included in that the building will continue at Har Homa," Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak said.
Palestinians insist peace talks can restart only when Israel halts work on a new settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on a hill called Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic.

All eyes have turned to U.S. President Bill Clinton to put forward a new initiative to rescue the U.S.-sponsored Middle East peace process. Clinton has pledged renewed personal involvement to put peace moves back on track.
Israel demands Palestinian President Yasser Arafat crack down on "terrorism" as a condition for resuming peace talks.

"He and his commanders must fight against terrorism and deny all terrorism and all violence in the area. That is necessary for us to take more risk and to move forward with the peace," Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said in Washington on Thursday.

Netanyahu has charged Arafat gave Islamist militants a green light to launch attacks such as a suicide bombing that killed three Israelis two weeks ago and a pair of botched suicide blasts in Gaza this week. Arafat denied the allegation.
The military wing of the Islamic Jihad group on Thursday claimed responsibility for the Gaza bombings. Jihad sources said the Palestinian Authority had arrested 30 of their activists.

Backing away from enflaming Moslem militants further, Netanyahu's office said Israel had suspended its request the United States extradite Moussa Abu Marzook, a politburo member of the Islamic group Hamas.
Security sources said Israel feared the extradition would spark a wave of attacks in the Jewish state and harm its struggle against Islamists.
In the 15th consecutive day of West Bank violence, Palestinian students in Bethlehem rained stones on Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint while staging a mock funeral for peace.
Protesters set alight a black coffin with a dove and olive branch inscribed with the words "Killed by Netanyahu".
Israeli soldiers dispersed the protesters with teargas and rubber bullets. No injuries were reported.

Netanyahu's office said it was still unclear whether Netanyahu, due to meet Clinton at the White House on Monday, would visit Jordan's King Hussein on Sunday in Minnesota where the monarch is to undergo surgery. Earlier, a spokesman for Netanyahu said the Israeli leader would travel to Minnesota.
King Hussein met Clinton and held talks with senior U.S. officials in Washington this week.

Osama el-Baz, a senior adviser to Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak, said in Cairo a U.S. peace initiative would "go down the drain" unless it required Israel to refrain from unilateral steps on Jerusalem.
Jewish settlers, who helped propel Netanyahu to power last year, urged the right-wing prime minister not to give in to "terrorism" by agreeing to a settlement freeze.
"The fixed ritual that concessions are needed in order to stop acts of murder will lead to more acts of terror," the YESHA Jewish settler council wrote in a letter to Netanyahu.
YESHA said it also sent a letter to U.S. Ambassador Martin Indyk protesting "the U.S. president's intention to dictate to the Israeli government" on its settlement policy.
